597105.old:
Catalytic hydrogenation of aldehydes and ketones

Hydrogen (\(\ce{H2}\)) reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols in the presence of a metal catalyst such as finely divided \(\ce{Ni}\), \(\ce{Pd}\) or \(\ce{Pt}\), as shown in the following examples.
597105.new:
Writing reduction as [H]

A reducing agent, written [H] over the arrow, reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols: one H adds to the carbonyl carbon and one H adds to the oxygen, as shown in the following examples.

597105.old: If a \(\ce{C=C}\) bond and a \(\ce{C=O}\) bond are present in the same molecule, catalytic hydrogenation reduces both, as shown below.
597105.new: Do not confuse reduction with hydrogenation. Hydrogenation (Section 3.4) is H2 with a metal catalyst (Ni, Pd or Pt) adding across a C=C; reduction ([H]) turns a C=O into C–OH. When a molecule has both a C=C and a C=O, H2 with a metal catalyst adds to both, as shown below.

597105.new: In the laboratory a common reducing agent is a hydride reagent such as sodium borohydride (NaBH<sub>4</sub>); in the body it is NADH (Chapter 13). Whatever the reagent,

597105.new: Write [O] for any oxidizing agent and [H] for any reducing agent (such as NaBH<sub>4</sub>). Use [H] for a C=O becoming C–OH; H<sub>2</sub> with a Ni, Pd or Pt catalyst adding across a C=C is hydrogenation.
